title: Question 7: Voter Identification Requirement

context.text: Question 7 is Initiative Petition C-02-2023, a citizen-initiated amendment to Article 2 of the Nevada Constitution. Under Article 19, Section 2 of the Nevada Constitution, an initiative to amend the Constitution must be approved by voters at two successive general elections; this is the second vote, after November 2024, per the Legislative Counsel Bureau fiscal note. The Nevada Independent reports the petition was filed by Repair the Vote, a political action committee led by former Clark County Republican Party chair David Gibbs.

News 3/News 4 reports voter ID passed in 2024 by over 46 percentage points. It is one of two statewide questions on the Nov. 3, 2026 ballot, the fewest since 2012 per News 3/News 4, and it keeps its 2024 number.
The Nevada Secretary of State's office released its official 2026 Ballot Question Guide on or about Sept. 29-30, 2026, per FOX5.
The Nevada Independent reported in 2024 that a Carson City judge dismissed a lawsuit seeking to block the petition in February 2024 and the Nevada Supreme Court upheld that ruling in April 2024.

question.text: Should the Nevada Constitution be amended to require voters to either present photo identification to verify their identity when voting in-person or to provide certain personal information to verify their identity when voting by mail ballot?

summary.text: Initiative Petition C-02-2023 would add Sections 1B and 1C to Article 2 of the Nevada Constitution. In-person voters (early voting or Election Day) would show an ID that is current or not expired for more than four years; a voter more than 70 years old could use an ID expired for any length of time. Accepted IDs include a Nevada driver's license; an ID card issued by Nevada, another state or the U.S. government; certain government employee photo IDs; a U.S. passport; a U.S. military ID; a student photo ID from a Nevada public college, university or technical school; tribal photo ID; a Nevada concealed firearms permit; and other government-issued photo ID the Legislature may approve. Mail voters would provide the last four digits of their Nevada driver's license number, or of their Social Security number if they have no Nevada license, or the number the county clerk provided at registration if they have neither. Under current law, only certain voters (those who registered by mail or computer and have not voted in a Nevada federal election, and online registrants within 14 days of an election) must show identification. The digest says that if approved again in 2026, the Legislature could enact related laws in the 2027 session and the changes would take effect for the 2028 election cycle. Fiscal note (Legislative Counsel Bureau Fiscal Analysis Division, July 29, 2024): financial impact is stated as "Yes"; the Secretary of State's Office estimated about $6,750 to change voter systems by 2028, and the cost to the State or local governments of providing a free alternative identity document to voters without an accepted ID cannot be determined with any reasonable degree of certainty.

measure.yesMeans: A "Yes" vote would amend Article 2 of the Nevada Constitution to require in-person Nevada voters present certain identification and mail ballot voters to provide certain information in order to cast a legal ballot.
measure.noMeans: A "No" vote would keep the Nevada Constitution in its current form.

argumentsFor.text: Ballot Question Committee in favor (David Gibbs, Chair; Chuck Muth; David O'Mara): "Requiring voters to show a photo ID before voting is a sensible and effective step to help make our elections more secure and to give people more confidence in the results."
Ballot Question Committee in favor (David Gibbs, Chair; Chuck Muth; David O'Mara): "A photo ID requirement will help people trust our election system and make sure that every vote is valid."

argumentsAgainst.text: Ballot Question Committee opposed (Jennifer Fleischmann Willoughby, Chair; Daniel Bravo; Jessica Rodriguez): "The ID requirements in Question 7 will mean fewer eligible people will cast ballots, while the new law would do nothing to prevent voter fraud."

Ballot Question Committee opposed (Jennifer Fleischmann Willoughby, Chair; Daniel Bravo; Jessica Rodriguez): "Voters living in rural or tribal communities will have to travel long distances to a DMV to receive an ID."

currentLaw.text: Under current law Nevada voters must show identification only in limited situations tied to how and when they registered: voters who registered (or preregistered) by mail or computer and have not previously voted in a Nevada federal election, and voters who register online less than 14 days before an election, who must vote in person with identification and proof of residency. Nevada otherwise verifies voters by signature.

fiscalImpact.text: Fiscal Analysis Division, Legislative Counsel Bureau (July 29, 2024): financial impact is stated as "Yes." The Secretary of State's Office estimated about $6,750 to modify voter check-in, mail-ballot verification and the voter registration system in time for 2028. The Division assumes the Legislature would provide an alternative identity document at no cost to voters without an accepted ID, borne by the State or local governments, and the cost cannot be determined with any reasonable degree of certainty.

supporters.text: Repair the Vote (PAC led by David Gibbs, former Clark County GOP chair, which filed the petition)
Nevada Voter ID Coalition (committee chaired by Gov. Joe Lombardo, per The Nevada Independent in 2024)
Yea7Nay6DotNet (Reno committee created to support Question 7 and oppose Question 6)
Ballot Question Committee in favor: David Gibbs (Chair), Chuck Muth, David O'Mara

opponents.text: Nevada Voter Freedom Alliance (PAC formed by Battle Born Progress)
Ballot Question Committee opposed: Jennifer Fleischmann Willoughby (Chair), Daniel Bravo, Jessica Rodriguez

campaignFinance.text: Through the first half of 2026 (reports covering January-June, per The Nevada Independent, July 23, 2026): Repair the Vote (supports) had raised $3,000 in 2026 from one donor; Nevada Voter ID Coalition (supports) reported no contributions this year and spent $3,000 on consulting; Nevada Voter Freedom Alliance (opposes) reported no contributions this cycle and spent $2,400 on consulting. In the 2024 cycle Better Nevada PAC received $1.5 million from Las Vegas Sands and passed $1.4 million of it to its offshoot, now the Nevada Voter ID Coalition and Repair the Vote raised more than $300,000; the opposition PAC raised $60,000. The July-September report was due Oct. 15 and was not found.

researchNotes: Sources: nvsos.gov is behind bot protection (not bypassed); the official text was read instead from the Clark County Election Department's 'Ballot Questions, General Election November 3, 2026' PDF, which reproduces the question, Legislative Counsel explanation and digest, the Ballot Question Committee arguments and rebuttals, and the Fiscal Analysis Division fiscal note for both statewide questions. Note that the explanation/arguments/fiscal note in that 2026 county document are the 2024-era texts (fiscal notes dated July 29 and Aug. 1, 2024), since the same initiatives return unchanged for the second vote. Slate: the county document contains exactly two statewide questions (6 and 7); News 3/News 4 (July 2026) reports these are the only two statewide questions this year, with other petitions failing to qualify, and FOX5 (Sept. 30, 2026) reports the Secretary of State's official 2026 Ballot Question Guide covers these two. The nvsos.gov guide itself was not read. Arguments are excerpts of the official committee arguments (the pamphlet prints one argument for and one against, plus a rebuttal on each side), attributed to the committees as the document names them. Required vote: a majority of those voting at this second election. Campaign finance: from The Nevada Independent (July 23, 2026), covering reports filed through the first half of 2026; the Oct. 15 report (July-September) was not found, and the Secretary of State's Aurora campaign finance system is behind bot protection and was not accessed. Supporter and opponent lists come from that reporting and from the committees named in the county document. The official full text of the initiative petition was not located outside the Secretary of State's protected site.
